extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in the history and practice of advertising (especially 18th–19th century British advertising)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical examples concerning the wording, placement, and running of matrimonial advertisements and related agency services (also examples of lottery advertising tactics). Focus is on what advertisers included, how agencies managed matches, fee/operational practices, and persuasive devices used in ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of urgent timing language in lottery ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ words and phrases indicating immediacy and finality (e.g., 'This Day', 'To-morrow', 'the last of all', 'all Lotteries end in this kingdom') to compel immediate purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the Times and contractors' notices repeatedly inserted 'to-morrow'/'this day' and 'last' language. The publisher's specimen reads: 'This Day, a Ticket must gain . . .' — urgency was used as a primary sales driver in the final State lottery appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear statement of prize structure and amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: List the prizes and their amounts explicitly (e.g., 'Six prizes of 30,000!., and every other prize amounting to 389,000!.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lottery adverts presented exact prize breakdowns (ticket/half/quarter/eighth/sixteenth gains). Such specific monetary claims were central to the persuasive appeal of lottery advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give sales locations and office addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide precise offices/addresses where tickets and shares can be purchased (e.g., 'Swift and Co. . . . 11, Poultry; 1, Strand; and 31 Aldgate High-street').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting shopfront locations and multiple offices built credibility and allowed buyers to find sellers; lottery contractors repeatedly listed addresses in adverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite prior success / sold prizes to build credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers listed past prizes sold/shared by them (e.g., 'shared and sold, within the last 12 months, 5 prizes of 30,000!. and 9 of 20,000!.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractors bragged about previous big prizes they had sold as proof of competence and to reassure buyers; this functions as an early form of testimonial/evidence of track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of handbills, illustrations and verse for attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute eccentric handbills with illustrations and verses to attract public attention outside the scarce newspaper columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Bish's eccentric handbills and verses; when newspaper advertising space was limited, handbills and repetition of handbill distribution ('people were provided with waste paper for an indefinite period') were used to increase visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and prominent placement in newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat notices across dates and use prominent placements (front page/public notice) to counter apathy and ensure awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices were repeated (Oct 13, 16, 17) and sometimes placed as a public notice on the Times front page; repetition and placement were tactical choices to combat low sales or public apathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active rebuttal of rumors for credibility management
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish unequivocal denials/reassurances to refute damaging anonymous assertions (e.g., contractors assuring the public that no application for postponement had been made).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contractors' public assurance—'no such application has been made'—serves as an example of adverts functioning also as reputation/issue management statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of unfair expected-value and overpricing (Adam Smith's caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lotteries are typically priced above their fair statistical value; the chance of gain is overvalued by many purchasers, and buying more tickets increases expected loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adam Smith quoted: 'The tickets are really not worth the price which is paid by the original subscribers...' and 'the more tickets you adventure upon the more likely you are to be a loser.' This is an evaluative principle for assessing the fairness/ethics of lottery promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include personal particulars in matrimonial ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should set out situation in life, age, constitution, religion, and other particulars of the person (clear, accurate description encouraged by agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency copy instructed that 'the Situation in Life, the Age, Constitution, and Religion of the Party [be] set forth with all possible Accuracy and Candour.' Historical matrimonial adverts frequently enumerated these items to facilitate matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit financial requirements and incomes
rubrics_metrics.description: State income/financial expectations plainly and often in precise sums (e.g., women listing the exact sum they expect; gentlemen listing required bride income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage notes young ladies 'put down in plain figures the precise sum which they think their charms are worth' and gentlemen listing expected bride income or offering their own incomes (e.g., 'Constance is already possessed of £500 a year').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepayment requirement for newspaper adverts
rubrics_metrics.description: All advertisements must be prepaid before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical practice noted: when second steps are taken, communication is made through a newspaper of the same proprietary and 'all advertisements must be prepaid.' This is a procedural rule affecting ad placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency confidentiality, vetting, and secrecy assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: Matchmaking agencies promise secrecy, honour, and discretion and require evidence or 'best proof' of suitability ('well paid for it', 'Secrecie and Prudence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Houghton's notices emphasise managing matches 'with all the Honour and Secrecy imaginable' and promise careful vetting; agencies used these assurances to overcome public suspicion and to attract depositors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency operational practices and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify agency procedures: separate rooms for interviews, hours of operation, fee structure (e.g., Five Guineas on taking down minutes, no more until completion), and steps for agents acting on behalf of principals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dover Street marriage-agency copy lists opening hours, use of separate apartments, the five-guinea fee payable when minutes are taken, and that no further payment is due until completion—illustrating standard agency operating terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require accurate written particulars when principals cannot attend
rubrics_metrics.description: If a principal cannot attend in person, an agent should provide a written recital containing exact particulars to allow the managers to complete the business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advertisement advised that those who cannot attend 'are requested to signify their Intention by their Friend in Writing' and that such recital must be 'with the utmost Exactness.' This is a procedural criterion for agency intake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting / proof of means and status for entry to agency services
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies ask for proof of fortune/status and reserve services to suitable persons (phrases like 'None but a real Gentleman will succeed' and 'prove of being (totally) at their own disposal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dover Street's ad explicitly limits clientele and demands 'the best Proof of being (totally) at their own Disposal'—an example of gatekeeping/vetting criteria used to signal exclusivity and reduce misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal compliance and restrictions on lotteries/coupons
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and advertisers must be aware of statutory constraints (Lottery Act, Betting-House Act) that limit what papers can do; the Lottery Act extended to Scotland and was enforced by Home Office notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts that small papers offering coupons for lottery shares received warnings from the Home Office and had to discontinue, noting statutory reach (Lottery Act extends to Scotland) and later the Betting-House Extension Act 1874.
